Context & Motivation

Why Hybrid? The Problem With One Model

The Zero-Day Gap

Signature-based IDS fails on novel attacks — they cannot detect what they have never catalogued. Industrial IoT and enterprise networks face unknown threats daily.

Our Constraint

We train on benign traffic only. No attack labels seen during training. Any deviation from the learned normal distribution flags an intrusion — including zero-day patterns.

The Single-Model Trade-Off

A deep autoencoder achieves excellent anomaly ranking (AUC 0.8965) but needs threshold tuning for precision. A random forest alone (AUC 0.34) can't learn without labels. Neither model alone solves both problems.

The Hybrid Solution

Two complementary roles, one pipeline:

DL Layer

Autoencoder learns a compact (68→32-dim) representation of normal traffic. High reconstruction error = anomalous flow. Provides the anomaly score.

ML Layer

Random Forest is trained on AE-generated pseudo-labels. It learns explicit tree-based decision boundaries using raw traffic features — providing precision the AE cannot.

PHASE PROGRESSION
Baseline ML → Advanced ML → DL (AE) → Hybrid ← Now

Loss: MSE(input, output) Optimizer: Adam lr=1e-3 39,908 parameters Batch: 512 · Epochs: 50 (best: 48)

How Anomalies Are Detected

The AE is trained to reconstruct benign flows with low error. At inference, attack traffic produces high Mean Squared Error — it doesn't fit the learned normal manifold. We flag flows above the P99 threshold (calibrated on benign validation set).

Training Strategy

RobustScaler fitted on benign-only data. Clipped to [-10, 10]. EarlyStopping (patience=7) + ReduceLROnPlateau prevents overfitting. Best epoch automatically checkpointed.

04 / 13
DL Component

Autoencoder Variants — Why These Two?

Sparse Autoencoder

L1 Regularisation

What it does: Adds an L1 activity penalty (λ=1e-4) on the bottleneck layer. This forces most of the 32 latent neurons toward zero — only a handful of dimensions carry signal for any given flow.

Why Sparse AE — not another variant?

vs Variational AE (VAE): VAE adds stochastic sampling and a KL-divergence term. On tabular network data, the probabilistic bottleneck hurts reconstruction quality and makes the anomaly score less stable — not ideal for threshold-based IDS.

vs Contractive AE: Contractive AE penalises the Jacobian of the encoder — computationally expensive and harder to tune. L1 sparsity achieves similar "robust" latent space with a single scalar λ.

Why we chose it: Sparser activations make the latent space more separable. If an attack flow activates different neurons than all benign flows did during training, the anomaly boundary becomes sharper.

Result: Sparse AE achieves AUC=0.8929 — within 0.4% of baseline. The sparser bottleneck slightly changes the latent structure but doesn't improve the score alone.

Denoising Autoencoder

Gaussian Noise σ=0.1

What it does: A GaussianNoise(σ=0.1) Keras layer is inserted right after the input — active only during training, disabled at inference. The model must reconstruct the clean input from corrupted data.

Why Denoising AE — not another variant?

vs Masked AE (random feature dropout): Masking randomly zeroes features — too destructive for network flows where every feature has physical meaning. Gaussian corruption is gentler and theoretically justified.

vs plain Dropout in encoder: Internal dropout corrupts activations but not inputs. Denoising at the input level forces the encoder to learn invariant latent representations — more robust to noisy traffic measurements in production.

Why we chose it: Real IDS deployments have noisy sensors (packet loss, jitter). A noise-robust encoder generalises better to measurement noise. Our results confirm this — Denoising AE achieves the best F1 (0.1433) and recall (0.0785), 4× better than standard AE at the same operating threshold.

Star result: Denoising AE F1=0.1433 vs Standard AE F1=0.0336. Sacrifices only 1% AUC (0.8867 vs 0.8965) but 4× better F1 and recall — the most practically deployable variant.

05 / 13
ML Component

Random Forest — Why RF, Not OC-SVM or IF?

Random Forest (Chosen)

How it works here: AE threshold (P99) generates pseudo-labels for the full dataset — flows above threshold = pseudo-attack (1), below = pseudo-benign (0). RF trains on these labels using raw 68-dim features.

Why this is powerful: RF gets a directional signal — it learns "what does an AE-flagged flow look like in raw feature space?" and draws tree-based boundaries. It operates on the full feature space, not just the latent space.

n_estimators=200 max_depth=12 class_weight=balanced n_jobs=-1 (parallel)

AE + RF hybrid AUC = 0.7920 — the best performing true hybrid, with sharper boundaries at the P99 threshold than AE alone due to RF's feature-level splits.

OC-SVM (Tried & Rejected)

Problem 1 — Scale: OC-SVM with RBF kernel scales O(n²) in training. At 3M+ samples, even subsampling to 80K rows takes 20+ minutes per run on our t3.large (8GB RAM).

Problem 2 — Direction: OC-SVM is fully unsupervised — it doesn't use the AE's pseudo-labels. When its unsupervised score is blended 50/50 with the AE score, it dilutes the AE's strong anomaly signal.

Result: AUC drops from 0.8965 → 0.4600 when blended with AE.

Isolation Forest (Tried & Rejected)

Faster than OC-SVM (O(n log n)) but still fully unsupervised. Contamination parameter (5%) forces it to label some benign training points as anomalies, and when blended with AE scores at equal weight: AUC drops to 0.4231.

Unlike RF, IF cannot use the pseudo-label signal — it cannot learn what the AE considers anomalous.

Critical finding: Standard AE alone achieves the highest AUC (0.8965) and Avg Precision (0.7578). Adding OC-SVM or Isolation Forest to the blend halves the AUC because their unsupervised scores have no directional alignment with the AE's anomaly signal. Only the AE + RF combination maintains meaningful performance (0.7920) because RF is guided by AE pseudo-labels.

Discriminative Performance

ROC & Precision-Recall Curves

Standard AE (blue dashed, AUC=0.8965) dominates — its curve rises steeply before FPR=0.2, showing strong separation. AE+RF follows at 0.7920. All OC-SVM/IF/Ensemble curves cluster below the random 0.5 diagonal — equal-weight blending with weaker models actively destroys the AE's signal.

Class imbalance context: Random classifier AP = 0.36 (36% attack base rate). Standard AE maintains precision >0.75 across most recall values (AP=0.7578). AE+RF holds solid precision at ~0.60 (AP=0.5593). These two are the only models worth deploying.

The threshold trade-off: At P99, the ensemble correctly classifies 99% of benign flows but misses 99.5% of attacks. Lowering to P90 improves recall to ~70% (from AE's phase 2 analysis) — but requires rebalancing FPR for each deployment context. This is an operational tuning choice, not a model flaw.

10 / 13
Attack-Family Diagnostic

Per-Attack Detection Rate: AE vs Meta-Ensemble

✅ Detectable Attacks

DDOS-LOIC-UDP: ~100% — extreme volumetric attack floods create massive flow rate spikes. The AE reconstructs these very poorly (mean error 8.94 vs benign 0.08).

DoS Slowloris: ~73% — slow HTTP header attack keeps connections open abnormally long, creating unusual flow duration/byte patterns.

❌ Evasive Attacks

SSH Bruteforce, DoS-HOIC, Bot, Infiltration: ~0% — these attacks are engineered to mimic legitimate traffic at the flow-statistics level. Bot malware error (0.13) ≈ benign mean (0.08). Invisible to reconstruction-error IDS.

Interesting reversal: For DoS-Slowloris, Standard AE detects ~73% but the Meta-Ensemble drops to ~22%. OC-SVM/IF scores override the AE's sensitivity for this attack family — confirming that the ensemble blend is counterproductive.

11 / 13
Operational Analysis

Threshold Calibration & RF Feature Importance

Reading the Plot

■ Standard AE (dashed blue) offers a meaningful operating curve — at P90 (FPR=10%), TPR reaches 70%. Security operators can tune the threshold to balance alert volume vs coverage.

■ Meta-Ensemble (red) stays flat near 0% TPR across all thresholds — even at P90 (FPR=10%), it barely detects attacks. This makes it operationally non-viable as a deployment model.

Feature_0 dominates with Gini importance 0.107 — likely a flow-rate or byte-count statistic. Features 17, 19 follow at 0.063 each. The RF tree splits confirm the hybrid rationale: the AE learns the global manifold; the RF identifies specific threshold values on individual traffic statistics that the AE's reconstruction error cannot explicitly articulate.

Removing noise augmentation reduces F1 by 4× (0.0336 vs 0.1433). The GaussianNoise layer is what makes the Denoising AE the most practically useful variant — noise robustness translates directly to better threshold generalisation.

OC-SVM / IF ablation: Removing these from the ensemble and using AE+RF alone recovers AUC from 0.41 → 0.79. The lesson: equal-weight fusion of misaligned anomaly scores is actively harmful. Score fusion requires alignment of signal direction, not just concatenation.

Four Key Findings

1

Standard AE is the strongest anomaly ranker — AUC 0.8965, AP 0.7578. No hybrid variant improves on this metric. The AE's learned normal manifold is extremely informative.

2

AE + RF is the best practical hybrid — AUC 0.7920, sharper boundaries. RF only works because the AE provides the pseudo-label signal. Remove the AE and RF collapses to 0.34.

3

Denoising AE is most deployment-ready — 4× better F1, same AUC cost of 1%. Noise-robust encoder generalises to more attack families at threshold.

4

OC-SVM & IF damage the hybrid — equal-weight blending with undirected anomaly scores halves AUC. Score fusion requires directional alignment, not just concatenation.

Future Directions

→

Temporal / Sequence Modelling: LSTM or Transformer AE to capture flow sequences — targets SSH bruteforce, Bot, and Infiltration that evade flow-level analysis.

→

Concept Drift Detection: Evaluate models on temporally-shifted test windows (week-by-week). Measure AUC degradation over time and implement sliding-window retraining.

→

Adversarial Robustness: Apply FGSM perturbations to input features and measure how much an attacker must modify traffic statistics to evade each model.

→

Learned Score Fusion: Replace equal-weight α=0.5 blend with a trained meta-learner (gradient boost on AE score, RF probability, and bottleneck features). Aligns signal directions before fusion.

BOTTOM LINE

The two-stage hybrid design is validated: the AE provides the anomaly signal; the RF provides feature-level precision. The interaction is directional — the AE must come first. Reproducible, fully cached, extensible to future attack families.
